title: US Pressures Europe to Release Diesel Reserves Immediately as Trump Threatens Export Ban
excerpt: The Trump administration wants the EU to release 120 million barrels of diesel within six months — more than 40% of the bloc's emergency stocks — while President Trump weighs curbing US diesel exports to lower fuel prices before the midterms.
body:
• The Trump administration has told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel stocks or face a potential US diesel export ban, according to three sources cited by Reuters.
  • Washington has asked the EU to release 120 million barrels of diesel over six months — more than 40% of the bloc's current emergency gasoil and diesel reserves.
  • Trump is weighing curbs on US diesel exports to bring down fuel prices before November's midterm elections; US diesel averaged $6.39 a gallon on Thursday, up from $3.71 a year earlier.
  • Energy ministers from Britain and the EU held emergency talks Thursday that broke up without resolution, with Europe wary of leaving itself exposed if the Gulf crisis flares over winter.

The Trump administration has issued an ultimatum to Europe's biggest economies: release emergency diesel stocks, or face a US export ban on the fuel. Washington told Germany and France to draw down their diesel inventories to ease global fuel prices — or risk Washington restricting its own diesel exports — three people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.

The ask is enormous. A source in a European capital said the US wants the EU to release 120 million barrels of diesel in the next six months. That is more than 40% of the 39 million metric tons of emergency gasoil and diesel stocks EU member states currently hold, according to the latest available Eurostat data — roughly one month of total EU diesel and gasoil consumption.

Context & Background

The pressure comes as President Trump considers curbing US diesel exports to reduce fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections. Energy Secretary Chris Wright presented the plan to Europe as an alternative to an outright ban on US exports, according to Politico. Germany held 5.6 million tons and France 8.2 million tons of emergency stocks in May 2025 data, together about 35% of the EU's strategic reserves.

The backdrop is a global diesel market under severe strain from the US-Iran war and the war in Ukraine. Diesel prices have surged to record or near-record levels in several markets, including Europe, and the fuel underpins trucking, agriculture and industry. The average gallon of diesel in the US cost $6.39 on Thursday, up from $3.71 a year earlier, according to AAA. Europeans pay even more: the EU average was $9.53 a gallon, compared with roughly $7.11 before the Iran war began.

Impact & Analysis

Europe faces a painful balancing act. Having cut reliance on Russian fuel after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and reduced its own refining capacity over two decades, Europe has grown increasingly dependent on diesel imports from the US — especially as the Iran war slashes Middle East supplies. But complying with Washington's demand could leave the continent exposed if the Gulf crisis flares over the winter, with Houthi rebels threatening Red Sea shipping lanes.

Energy ministers and officials from the European Commission, Germany, France, Italy, Ireland and Britain held a call on October 1 to discuss a possible release of stocks, according to EU officials. A later emergency session involving Britain broke up without resolution. The UK is particularly exposed: it holds only about 40 days of diesel reserves and relies on the US for a quarter of its imports, with pump prices already above £2 a litre.

"We've lost some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we're restoring those, and we've lost diesel exports from China. So that's a lot of interruptions."

— Chris Wright, US Energy Secretary

Not everyone backs the ban idea. The American Petroleum Institute warned in a September 28 post that restricting exports "could disrupt refinery operations" and reduce fuel production. In March, the International Energy Agency already oversaw the release of 400 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves to address the supply disruption after the start of the Iran war.

Diaspora Angle

For the large Indian diaspora in Britain and continental Europe, a transatlantic diesel standoff translates directly into pump prices and heating costs as winter approaches — and any further supply squeeze feeds the same inflation that hits remittance-heavy households on both sides.

What's Next

Talks between EU and US officials could resume as soon as Friday, according to reports. The question is whether Europe negotiates a smaller, coordinated release through the IEA framework — or whether Trump follows through on the export ban threat first.
